time.desc: The two sides started indirect nuclear negotiations at a technical level at a neutral location under the mediation of a third party. At the same time, one side demonstrated deterrence with live-fire drills and short-term control of key straits.
One mainstream media revealed that its government internally discussed options for military strikes against its opponents’ nuclear facilities and assessed subsequent escalation paths.
The mediator publicly stated that the two countries were close to reaching a consensus on nuclear and sanctions arrangements, sending a diplomatic signal that "an agreement is in sight"

The two parties and their allies launched large-scale joint air strikes against their opponents and publicly named the operation. The conflict escalated from confrontation to open war, and the top leader of the opponent was confirmed dead after the first round of strikes.

For the first time, the side that launched the air strike publicly admitted that its personnel were killed and seriously injured in the opponent's counterattack, breaking the "zero casualties" narrative.
The party affected by the air attack completed the change of supreme power during the war and formally confirmed the new supreme leader to take office to maintain the continuity of the regime.
The warring parties carried out air strikes on facilities related to the opponent's key oil and gas export hubs, and the conflict further spilled over to energy supply risks.

One side made an official statement on its position on the navigation of key straits, saying that it has no objection to the passage of ships from some countries for the time being and hinted that it will adjust its energy market policy depending on the length of the conflict.
The leader of one party issued an ultimatum on the opening of key straits and threatened to attack the opponent's power and other civilian energy infrastructure to put pressure on

After the ultimatum, the two sides confirmed that they had started dialogue, and the party launching the air strikes announced that it would suspend attacks on its opponent's energy facilities to leave a short window for negotiations.
The party that launched the air strikes formally submitted a plan to end the conflict containing multiple clauses to its opponent in an attempt to push for a break in the ceasefire negotiations.
The party affected by the air attack completed a formal written response to the opponent's ceasefire plan, and the ceasefire negotiations entered a new stage.
Major powers outside the region jointly proposed a multi-point plan to end the war, calling for an immediate ceasefire and the restoration of normal traffic in key straits.

The leader of the side that launched the air strikes addressed the nation, declaring that he would crack down harder on his opponents within weeks and reaffirming plans to end the conflict in the short term.
The party launching the air strikes agreed to suspend bombing of its opponents and set a ceasefire window of about two weeks, and the market risk premium fell quickly.

After the ceasefire came into effect, the participating allies publicly stated that their military operations on specific fronts were not subject to the ceasefire, exposing the dispute over the scope of the ceasefire.

The party that launched air strikes during the ceasefire announced and initiated a naval blockade against its opponents, saying that it would not affect the freedom of navigation related to non-opponent ports.
The rival military launched a new missile offensive and fired missiles at an opponent's warship, while denying that it had closed the key strait.

For the first time, security figures from allies of the party launching the air strikes admitted that the air strikes lacked a feasible plan for regime change. The long-term success or failure of the war was said to depend on the whereabouts of a batch of highly enriched uranium.

When the leader of one country was interviewed, he questioned the life and death of his opponent's new supreme leader and said that the opponent's agreement terms were not good enough. The opponent issued an open letter stating that he was willing to negotiate with mutual respect but would not give in.
One of the opponent's highest-ranking officials (former speaker/secretary of an agency) was killed in an allied airstrike, becoming the highest-ranking official killed since the war began.

The coalition forces participating in the war launched a new round of air strikes on the opponent's giant natural gas fields at sea. Shipping in the key strait was effectively paralyzed, and international oil and gas prices rose in response.

The opponent's military statement warned that if the opponent carried out an attack on its energy facilities, it would completely close the key strait, and the opponent threatened "unprecedented bombing" and the imposition of tariffs.
Country Y and Country Z jointly attacked Country X Region D on a dock adjacent to Strait A, resulting in several casualties.
Leader A publicly called on all countries to go to Strait A to seize oil on their own, saying that Country X had been basically defeated, and related oil prices rose sharply.
Country Y and Country Z launch joint air strikes against the City C Petrochemical Special Economic Zone in the southwest of Country X, targeting its energy infrastructure
Leader A threatens to violently bomb Country X power plants, bridges and other civilian facilities, while Country X threatens to blockade Strait B in counterattack
Country X Activities were held in various places to commemorate the slain supreme leader, and the successor supreme leader made a strong speech and proposed to collect tolls for Strait A
Country Y The Navy began to mobilize troops to Strait A and prepare to implement a blockade of the Country X port, just as the two sides were meeting in City A
